entries.authors: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J.
entries.title: Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: tendon overuse injury, not a knee ligament sprain. Down one more for a single small study (38 patients). Result: low.
entries.population: adults with Achilles tendinopathy (38 patients) during a 12-month loading program
entries.takeaway: People who kept running and jumping during rehab, guided by a pain-monitoring model, improved as much over 12 months as those told to stop those activities for six weeks.

entries.authors: Smith BE, Hendrick P, Smith TO, et al.
entries.title: Should exercises be painful in the management of chronic musculoskeletal pain? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: The source itself rates short-term pain evidence as moderate (GRADE). Down one level for indirectness: chronic musculoskeletal pain, not a recent ligament sprain. Result: low.
entries.population: adults with chronic musculoskeletal pain in 7 randomized trials (385 participants)
entries.takeaway: Across seven trials in chronic musculoskeletal pain, exercise that was allowed to hurt somewhat gave a small short-term pain benefit over pain-free exercise and no clear difference later on.

entries.authors: Sprague AL, Couppé C, Pohlig RT, Snyder-Mackler L, Silbernagel KG.
entries.title: Pain-guided activity modification during treatment for patellar tendinopathy: a feasibility and pilot randomized clinical trial.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized pilot trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: tendon injury rather than ligament, and feasibility outcomes rather than clinical benefit. Down one more for a single very small study (15 people). Result: low.
entries.population: people aged 16-40 with patellar tendinopathy (15 enrolled) in a 12-week program
entries.takeaway: In a small pilot trial in patellar tendinopathy, running and jumping guided by the pain-monitoring model proved feasible, and treatment attendance looked higher than in the group told to avoid painful activity.

entries.authors: Thomeé R.
entries.title: A comprehensive treatment approach for patellofemoral pain syndrome in young women.
entries.startReason: The randomized comparison was isometric versus eccentric training and pain monitoring ran in both arms, so for this question it reads as an uncontrolled case series.
entries.gradeBasis: The randomized comparison was isometric versus eccentric training. The pain-monitoring system was used in both arms, so for this question the study acts as an uncontrolled case series and starts at very low. It is also indirect (patellofemoral pain) and small. Floor: very low.
entries.population: 40 women aged 15-28 with patellofemoral pain
entries.takeaway: A 12-week program for patellofemoral pain combining education, a pain-monitoring system and gradually progressed training was followed by less pain and better function, though pain monitoring itself was never tested against an alternative.

entries.authors: Grindem H, Snyder-Mackler L, Moksnes H, Engebretsen L, Risberg MA
entries.title: Simple decision rules can reduce reinjury risk by 84% after ACL reconstruction: the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort study.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (prospective cohort). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL), giving very low.
entries.population: 106 pivoting-sport athletes followed 2 years after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: After ACL surgery, athletes with more symmetrical quadriceps strength before returning to sport had fewer knee reinjuries; passing a battery of tests with every score above 90 was linked with lower risk, though that association was not statistically significant.

entries.authors: Losciale JM, Zdeb RM, Ledbetter L, Reiman MP, Sell TC
entries.title: The Association Between Passing Return-to-Sport Criteria and Second Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Risk: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: The review's own GRADE is very low (imprecision and heterogeneity). That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (ACLR population) changes nothing.
entries.population: patients returning to sport after ACL reconstruction (4 studies)
entries.takeaway: Pooling four studies, passing return-to-sport test batteries was not clearly linked with fewer second ACL injuries, and the authors rate this evidence as very low certainty.

entries.authors: Zhou W, Liu X, Hong Q, Wang J, Luo X.
entries.title: Association between passing return-to-sport testing and re-injury risk in patients after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of observational studies, so it starts at low (the abstract reports no GRADE rating). Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 1410 people after ACL reconstruction in 9 observational studies
entries.takeaway: Across nine studies after ACL reconstruction, passing return-to-sport testing was linked to roughly half the odds of graft rupture, but it was not linked to fewer knee injuries overall or fewer opposite-knee ACL injuries.

entries.authors: Piussi R, Simonson R, Zsidai B, et al.
entries.title: Better Safe Than Sorry? A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis on Time to Return to Sport After ACL Reconstruction as a Risk Factor for Second ACL Injury.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: The source itself rates the evidence very low (GRADE). It is also indirect (post-ACL reconstruction). Floor: very low.
entries.population: people returning to sport after ACL reconstruction (21 studies pooled)
entries.takeaway: People who went on to a second ACL injury had returned to sport about 25 days sooner than those who did not, though professionals showed no timing difference and certainty was very low.

entries.authors: van Melick N, van Cingel RE, Brooijmans F, et al.
entries.title: Evidence-based clinical practice update: practice guidelines for anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation based on a systematic review and multidisciplinary consensus.
entries.gradeBasis: A guideline built on a systematic review plus expert consensus. The abstract reports no certainty rating and the phase-structure recommendation rests mainly on consensus, so it is treated as expert opinion and starts at very low. It is also indirect (post-surgical ACL population). Floor: very low.
entries.population: adults in rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction (Dutch national guideline, 90 studies)
entries.takeaway: The Dutch guideline recommends rehabilitation in criterion-based phases (impairment-based work, then sport-specific training, then return to play), with strength, hop, movement-quality and psychological tests deciding each step.

entries.authors: Ardern CL, Glasgow P, Schneiders A, et al.
entries.title: 2016 Consensus statement on return to sport from the First World Congress in Sports Physical Therapy, Bern.
entries.gradeBasis: Expert consensus, so it starts at very low. It is also indirect: it covers athletes returning from any injury, not specifically a non-operative knee ligament sprain. Floor: very low.
entries.population: athletes returning to sport after any injury (17-expert consensus)
entries.takeaway: Experts agreed that return to sport is a continuum running alongside rehab, best decided together by athlete and clinicians who weigh risk, and noted that research to guide these decisions is scarce.

entries.authors: Svantesson J, Piussi R, Weissglas E, Svantesson E, Horvath A, Börjesson E, Williams A, Prill R, Samuelsson K, Hamrin Senorski E
entries.title: Shedding light on the non-operative treatment of the forgotten side of the knee: rehabilitation of medial collateral ligament injuries-a systematic review.
entries.gradeBasis: The review's own GRADE is very low (non-randomized studies, risk of bias), confirmed in the full text. That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (isolated MCL, not multi-ligament, not specifically field-sport athletes) changes nothing.
entries.population: 1,912 patients with isolated MCL injuries treated without surgery (26 reports, mostly before 2000)
entries.takeaway: Non-surgical care of grade I-II MCL sprains generally allowed early weight bearing and strengthening, but the programmes were poorly described and the evidence is very low certainty; complete immobilization was linked with quadriceps shrinkage.

entries.authors: Eitzen I, Moksnes H, Snyder-Mackler L, Risberg MA.
entries.title: A progressive 5-week exercise therapy program leads to significant improvement in knee function early after anterior cruciate ligament injury.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: Uncontrolled prospective cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: ACL rupture, not a multi-ligament sprain. Result: very low.
entries.population: 100 people within 3 months of ACL injury, as pre-surgery rehab or the first step of non-operative care
entries.takeaway: A 5-week progressive exercise program started within three months of ACL injury was well tolerated (about 4% adverse events) and improved strength, hop performance and self-reported knee function.

entries.authors: Filbay SR, Bullock G, Russell S, Brown F, Hui W, Egerton T.
entries.title: No Difference in Return-to-Sport Rate or Activity Level in People with Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Injury Managed with ACL Reconstruction or Rehabilitation Alone: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: The source rates the evidence low to very low (GRADE). Down one level for indirectness: complete ACL rupture, not a multi-ligament sprain. Floor: very low.
entries.population: people with ACL rupture managed by reconstruction or by rehabilitation alone (15 studies, 2 randomized)
entries.takeaway: Pooling 15 studies, people managed with rehabilitation alone after ACL rupture returned to sport at rates similar to those who had reconstruction, though certainty was low to very low and confounding was common.

entries.authors: Murray IR, Makaram NS, Geeslin AG, et al.
entries.title: Multiligament knee injury (MLKI): an expert consensus statement on nomenclature, diagnosis, treatment and rehabilitation.
entries.gradeBasis: Expert Delphi consensus, so it starts at very low. It is also indirect: it addresses multiligament injuries managed mostly with surgery, not a non-operative sprain in a field-sport athlete. Floor: very low.
entries.population: patients with multiligament knee injuries (39-member international Delphi panel from 14 countries)
entries.takeaway: A 39-member international Delphi panel agreed on terminology and care for multiligament knee injuries, including that the literature generally favours surgery for them, especially in young patients.

entries.authors: Diermeier T, Rothrauff BB, Engebretsen L, et al.
entries.title: Treatment after anterior cruciate ligament injury: Panther Symposium ACL Treatment Consensus Group.
entries.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
entries.gradeBasis: Expert consensus, so it starts at very low. It is also indirect (ACL rupture). Floor: very low.
entries.population: people with ACL injury choosing operative or non-operative care (66-expert consensus)
entries.takeaway: Experts recommended early reconstruction for highly active people in jumping, cutting and pivoting sports, mainly to protect meniscus and cartilage; structured rehab alone suits straight-line activity, and persistent instability or giving way points to surgery.

entries.authors: Sturgill LP, Snyder-Mackler L, Manal TJ, Axe MJ.
entries.title: Interrater reliability of a clinical scale to assess knee joint effusion.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: Measurement-reliability study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: a clinician-graded stroke test, not self-observed swelling the morning after loading. A single study as well. Result: very low.
entries.population: 75 outpatients aged 16-65 with a one-sided knee problem
entries.takeaway: Physical therapists grading knee swelling on a five-point stroke-test scale agreed well with each other (kappa 0.75) in 75 knee outpatients, and the authors present effusion as a signal for program progression.

entries.authors: Palmieri-Smith RM, Villwock M, Downie B, Hecht G, Zernicke R.
entries.title: Pain and effusion and quadriceps activation and strength.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized crossover, so it starts at high; down one for indirectness (healthy knees, induced swelling), down one for a single small study (14). Result: low.
entries.population: 14 healthy volunteers with experimentally induced knee pain and/or swelling
entries.takeaway: In 14 healthy volunteers, induced knee pain and induced knee swelling each reduced quadriceps strength and activation by a similar amount, but having both together did not deepen the deficit.

entries.authors: Kikuchi N, Kanamori A, Arai N, Okuno K, Yamazaki M.
entries.title: Joint Effusion at 3 Months After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: Its Risk Factors and Association With Subsequent Muscle Strength and Graft Remodeling.
entries.gradeBasis: Retrospective case-control study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL knees. Result: very low.
entries.population: 174 patients 3 months after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: After ACL reconstruction, marked joint effusion at three months was independently linked to weaker quadriceps symmetry at six months and slower graft maturation on MRI at one year.

entries.authors: Huang J, Song B, Lin G, He Z, Zhang C, Fu SN.
entries.title: Joint effusion after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: Associations with higher postoperative physical activity, patella alta and increased quadriceps tension.
entries.gradeBasis: Cross-sectional study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL knees. Result: very low.
entries.population: 119 adults 3-24 months after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In 119 people after ACL reconstruction, more weekly physical activity went with higher MRI effusion grades at 3 and 24 months, and lingering effusion went with stiffer quadriceps beyond a year.

entries.authors: Rambaud AJM, Ardern CL, Thoreux P, Regnaux JP, Edouard P
entries.title: Criteria for return to running after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review.
entries.gradeBasis: A scoping review of mostly non-randomized reports that catalogs criteria rather than testing whether they work, so it starts at low (not a review of RCTs). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL), giving very low.
entries.population: published rehab protocols and studies for adults after primary ACL reconstruction (201 studies)
entries.takeaway: Most protocols cleared running on time alone, typically around 12 weeks after surgery; fewer than one in five added clinical, strength or hop criteria, and where they did, symmetry above 70% was the usual threshold.

entries.authors: Sayer TA, van Melick N, Riera J, et al.
entries.title: Is it time to develop specific return to running criteria for ACL rehabilitation? An international survey of physiotherapists criteria for return to running following ACL injury.
entries.journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Cross-sectional survey, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: it reports what clinicians do, not whether it works, and covers ACL rather than multi-ligament injury. Result: very low.
entries.population: 476 physiotherapists in Australia, the Netherlands and France describing their practice after ACL injury, with or without surgery
entries.takeaway: Surveyed physiotherapists most often cleared running after ACL injury, operated or not, on swelling, pain, quadriceps strength and single-leg squat; common cut-offs were pain 0-3/10 and minimal swelling, but agreement was weak.

entries.authors: Coleman M, Burke R, Augustin F, et al.
entries.title: Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: healthy trained lifters, and a full training break rather than reduced sets. Down one more for a single small study. Result: low.
entries.population: 39 healthy resistance-trained young adults on a 9-week program
entries.takeaway: In trained young adults, a one-week complete training break midway through nine weeks of lifting did not change muscle growth, power or endurance, but lower-body strength gains were smaller than with continuous training.

entries.authors: Pancar Z, Ilhan MT, Darendeli MK, et al.
entries.title: Effects of deload periods in resistance training on muscle hypertrophy and strength endurance in untrained young men using a randomized within subject design.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized within-subject trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: healthy untrained men, not injury rehab. Down one more for a single small study (19 people). Result: low.
entries.population: 19 untrained young men, one limb per condition, over 8 weeks
entries.takeaway: Cutting sets and frequency in weeks 4 and 8 of an 8-week program did not reduce muscle growth or strength-endurance compared with continuous training, in a within-person trial of 19 untrained men.

entries.authors: Bell L, Strafford BW, Coleman M, Androulakis Korakakis P, Nolan D.
entries.title: Integrating Deloading into Strength and Physique Sports Training Programmes: An International Delphi Consensus Approach.
entries.gradeBasis: Expert Delphi consensus, so it starts at very low. It is also indirect: strength sport coaching, not rehab. Floor: very low.
entries.population: expert strength and physique coaches (21-34 per Delphi round)
entries.takeaway: Strength and physique coaches agreed on design principles for deloading and defined it as a deliberate stretch of lighter training meant to reduce fatigue, support recovery and ready athletes for the next block.

entries.authors: Buckthorpe M.
entries.title: Optimising the Late-Stage Rehabilitation and Return-to-Sport Training and Testing Process After ACL Reconstruction.
entries.gradeBasis: Narrative review, so it starts at very low. It is also indirect (post-ACL reconstruction). Floor: very low.
entries.population: athletes in late-stage rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: This narrative review argues that late rehab after ACL reconstruction should rebuild explosive strength, movement quality under fatigue, sport-specific skills and chronic training load before return to sport.

entries.authors: Fältström A, Gustafsson T, Hermansen A, Sonesson S.
entries.title: On-field rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament injury in contact team sports: a scoping review of exercises, progression and key principles.
entries.gradeBasis: Scoping review of mostly descriptive sources with no pooled trial outcomes, so it is treated as observational and starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: ACL injury, mainly football, and it describes practice rather than outcomes. Result: very low.
entries.population: athletes returning to contact team sports after ACL injury or reconstruction (38 mostly descriptive sources)
entries.takeaway: Across 38 mostly descriptive sources, on-field rehab for contact team sports moved through 2-5 stages from straight-line running to sport-specific practice, progressing on criteria such as minimal pain and swelling and adequate strength.

entries.authors: Della Villa F, Picinini F, Di Paolo S, et al.
entries.title: The impact of on-field rehabilitation on return to play and ACL re-injury risk after ACL reconstruction in football (soccer) players: A study on 401 consecutive cases.
entries.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
entries.gradeBasis: Retrospective cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL, football. Result: very low.
entries.population: 401 male football players after primary ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: Among 401 footballers after ACL reconstruction, more on-field rehab volume, frequency and compliance went with higher odds of returning to play at their previous level, though overall second-injury risk was not linked.

entries.authors: Pamboris GM, Pavlou K, Paraskevopoulos E, Mohagheghi AA
entries.title: Effect of open vs. closed kinetic chain exercises in ACL rehabilitation on knee joint pain, laxity, extensor muscles strength, and function: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
entries.journal: Frontiers in sports and active living
entries.gradeBasis: The review's own GRADE rates the quadriceps strength comparisons very low, each from a single trial (Tables 8 and 9). That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (ACL populations, not a non-operative multi-ligament sprain) changes nothing.
entries.population: adults after ACL reconstruction and adults with ACL-deficient knees (9 randomized trials)
entries.takeaway: Machine knee extensions (open chain) gave somewhat larger quadriceps strength gains than closed-chain work at 3-4 months in single small trials, without clear harm to knee laxity, though certainty is very low.

entries.authors: Perriman A, Leahy E, Semciw AI
entries.title: The Effect of Open- Versus Closed-Kinetic-Chain Exercises on Anterior Tibial Laxity, Strength, and Function Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: The review reports low- to moderate-certainty GRADE evidence. We take the lower bound, low, because outcome-level ratings are not in the abstract, then downgrade one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL population).
entries.population: adults after ACL reconstruction (10 randomized trials)
entries.takeaway: Across randomized trials after ACL surgery, adding open-chain quadriceps work early or late made no clear difference to knee laxity, strength or reported function compared with closed-chain work.

entries.authors: Escamilla RF, Fleisig GS, Zheng N, Barrentine SW, Wilk KE, Andrews JR
entries.title: Biomechanics of the knee during closed kinetic chain and open kinetic chain exercises.
entries.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (observational lab study). Down one level for indirectness (healthy knees, modeled forces rather than clinical outcomes), giving very low. The single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 10 healthy men in a lab, lifting at their 12-rep max (squat, leg press, knee extension)
entries.takeaway: In healthy lifters, squats and leg press loaded the PCL more as the knee bent deeper, while ACL tension appeared only in knee extensions near full straightening, so each exercise stresses different ligaments at different angles.

entries.authors: Escamilla RF
entries.title: Knee biomechanics of the dynamic squat exercise.
entries.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
entries.gradeBasis: Narrative review, so it starts at very low, which is the floor. It is indirect because it covers healthy knees and modeled forces.
entries.population: biomechanics studies of the squat, mostly in healthy adults
entries.takeaway: Knee forces in the squat rise as the knee bends, so a shallow range (roughly 0-50 degrees) keeps loads lowest for rehab; the squat does not destabilize the knee and works the quadriceps, hamstrings and calves together.

entries.authors: Kassiano W, Nunes JP, Costa B, Ribeiro AS, Loenneke JP, Cyrino ES
entries.title: Comparison of Muscle Growth and Dynamic Strength Adaptations Induced by Unilateral and Bilateral Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at high (meta-analysis of randomized trials judged with RoB 2). Down one level for indirectness (uninjured adults, not knee rehab), giving moderate. The review itself notes moderate risk of bias and limited literature.
entries.population: healthy adults in resistance-training trials (9 studies)
entries.takeaway: Single-leg and two-leg training built similar muscle size, but strength gains followed specificity: single-leg training improved single-leg strength more, and two-leg training improved two-leg strength more.

entries.authors: Graham M, Gohil A, Janatova T, Johnson D, Noehren B
entries.title: Compensatory Movement Strategies during the Rearfoot Elevated Split Squat after ACL Reconstruction.
entries.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (cross-sectional lab study). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL), giving very low. The single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 25 adults about 4 months after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: Compared with the other leg in the rear-foot-elevated (Bulgarian) split squat, the operated leg carried less load and its knee took a smaller share of the effort, shifting work to its hip and ankle; a more upright trunk increased offloading.

entries.authors: Wellsandt E, Failla MJ, Snyder-Mackler L
entries.title: Limb Symmetry Indexes Can Overestimate Knee Function After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (prospective cohort). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL), giving very low. A single modest-sized study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 70 athletes tested before and 6 months after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: Because the uninjured leg also weakens after surgery, side-to-side percentages can look better than true recovery; comparing against pre-surgery values of the uninjured leg flagged more athletes who went on to a second ACL injury.

entries.authors: Nagai T, Schilaty ND, Laskowski ER, Hewett TE
entries.title: Hop tests can result in higher limb symmetry index values than isokinetic strength and leg press tests in patients following ACL reconstruction.
entries.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (cross-sectional comparison). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL), giving very low. The single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 26 adults about 8 months after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In the same patients, hop tests, especially the triple hop, gave higher symmetry scores than isokinetic strength or leg press power tests; strength tests expose deficits that hops can mask, and a unilateral leg press can isolate the weaker leg.

entries.authors: Clark NC, Reilly LJ, Davies SC
entries.title: Intra-rater reliability, measurement precision, and inter-test correlations of 1RM single-leg leg-press, knee-flexion, and knee-extension in uninjured adult agility-sport athletes: Considerations for right and left unilateral measurements in knee injury control.
entries.journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (measurement-reliability study). Down one level for indirectness (uninjured athletes; 1RM, not 8RM), giving very low. The single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 13 uninjured adult agility-sport athletes
entries.takeaway: A single-leg leg press one-rep max was highly repeatable in agility-sport athletes, though precision differed between legs; leg press, leg curl and leg extension shared only about a third of their variance, so each tests something different.

entries.authors: Girdwood M, Culvenor AG, Rio EK, Patterson BE, Haberfield M, Couch J, Mentiplay B, Hedger M, Crossley KM
entries.title: Tale of quadriceps and hamstring muscle strength after ACL reconstruction: a systematic review with longitudinal and multivariate meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (meta-analysis of observational studies). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL), giving very low.
entries.population: adults 18-40 after primary ACL reconstruction (232 studies, about 34,000 people)
entries.takeaway: After ACL surgery, thigh strength improved fast at first and then plateaued around 12-18 months; on average, quadriceps strength was still more than 10% below the other leg at one year, and comparing with the other leg understated deficits.

entries.authors: Kyritsis P, Bahr R, Landreau P, Miladi R, Witvrouw E
entries.title: Likelihood of ACL graft rupture: not meeting six clinical discharge criteria before return to sport is associated with a four times greater risk of rupture.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (cohort). Down one level for indirectness (post-surgical ACL, elite males), giving very low.
entries.population: 158 male professional athletes returning to sport after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: Professional athletes who returned without meeting all six strength and hop criteria had about four times the graft rupture risk; a weaker hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio on the operated leg also carried higher risk.

entries.authors: Girdwood M, Culvenor AG, Patterson B, Haberfield M, Rio EK, Hedger M, Crossley KM
entries.title: No sign of weakness: a systematic review and meta-analysis of hip and calf muscle strength after anterior cruciate ligament injury.
entries.gradeBasis: The review's own GRADE is very low for all outcomes. That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (ACL population) changes nothing.
entries.population: adults 18-40 after ACL injury, mostly within a year of reconstruction (28 studies)
entries.takeaway: Unlike the 10-20% thigh deficits seen after ACL injury, hip and calf strength showed no consistent weakness versus the other leg or controls, so the authors advise checking each person rather than assuming deficits.

entries.authors: Nascimento LR, Teixeira-Salmela LF, Souza RB, Resende RA
entries.title: Hip and Knee Strengthening Is More Effective Than Knee Strengthening Alone for Reducing Pain and Improving Activity in Individuals With Patellofemoral Pain: A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis.
entries.journal: The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: Not a review of RCTs only: the abstract says it pooled randomized and/or controlled trials (14 trials), so non-randomized controlled trials are admitted, and it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness (patellofemoral pain, not a ligament sprain), giving very low. The source reports no GRADE rating.
entries.population: people with patellofemoral (kneecap) pain, 14 trials, 673 participants
entries.takeaway: For kneecap pain, adding hip strengthening to knee strengthening reduced pain and improved activity more than knee work alone, even though measured strength did not change significantly.

entries.authors: Xiao J, Feng C, Chu J, Zhao W, Zhang B, Yuan X
entries.title: Proximal core strengthening training for anterior cruciate ligament injury prevention with biomechanical improvements in knee/hip kinematics and strength gains: a systematic review and meta-analysis of low-certainty evidence.
entries.gradeBasis: The review's own GRADE is low for all outcomes (confirmed in the full-text limitations). Down one level for indirectness (mixed high-risk and post-ACL groups, biomechanical outcomes), giving very low.
entries.population: people at high ACL-injury risk, including some after ACL injury or reconstruction (24 studies, 749 participants)
entries.takeaway: Hip and trunk (proximal) strengthening may improve thigh strength and knee and hip movement control in people at higher ACL risk, though the certainty is low and injury prevention itself was not shown.

entries.authors: Cashman G, White C, Stephens R, Hoggs-Johnson S, Kissel J
entries.title: The effect of hip abductor or external rotator strength on dynamic knee valgus in healthy subjects-a systematic review with partial meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (review of cross-sectional studies). Down one level for indirectness (healthy people, not injured knees), giving very low.
entries.population: healthy adults without knee symptoms (22 studies)
entries.takeaway: In healthy people, weaker hip abductors or external rotators were mostly not linked with more inward knee collapse in movement tests, so hip weakness may not be the main driver of knee valgus.

entries.authors: Harøy J, Clarsen B, Wiger EG, Øyen MG, Serner A, Thorborg K, Hölmich P, Andersen TE, Bahr R
entries.title: The Adductor Strengthening Programme prevents groin problems among male football players: a cluster-randomised controlled trial.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at high (cluster RCT). Down one level for indirectness (uninjured footballers, groin rather than knee outcome), giving moderate. The trial is large, so no imprecision downgrade.
entries.population: 652 semiprofessional male football players from 35 teams
entries.takeaway: A single-exercise Copenhagen adduction programme, done three times weekly in preseason and weekly in season, cut the prevalence of groin problems by roughly 40% compared with usual training.

entries.authors: van Dyk N, Behan FP, Whiteley R
entries.title: Including the Nordic hamstring exercise in injury prevention programmes halves the rate of hamstring injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of 8459 athletes.
entries.gradeBasis: Not a review of RCTs: the headline pooled estimate mixes randomized and non-randomized designs (a reappraisal found only 5 of the 15 truly randomized), so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness (uninjured athletes, hamstring-strain outcome), giving very low.
entries.population: athletes across many sports (15 studies, 8,459 athletes)
entries.takeaway: Programmes that included Nordic hamstring exercises had about half the hamstring injuries of comparison groups, and the effect held when higher-bias studies were removed.

entries.authors: Impellizzeri FM, McCall A, van Smeden M
entries.title: Why methods matter in a meta-analysis: a reappraisal showed inconclusive injury preventive effect of Nordic hamstring exercise.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at high (meta-analysis restricted to RCTs). Down one level for indirectness (uninjured athletes, hamstring outcome), giving moderate. The authors give only conditional GRADE recommendations and describe the trials as mostly high risk of bias, which the rule does not downgrade for, so read this grade cautiously.
entries.population: athletes in randomized trials of Nordic hamstring exercise (6 RCTs)
entries.takeaway: Re-analysing only the truly randomized trials, the protective effect of Nordic hamstring exercise was uncertain, with wide intervals, so the benefit is plausible but not established.

entries.authors: Crawford SK, Sandberg C, Vlisides J, Thompson Q, Mosiman SJ, Heiderscheit BC, Hickey JT
entries.title: Hamstrings Muscle Architecture and Morphology Following 6 wk of an Eccentrically Biased Romanian Deadlift or Nordic Hamstring Exercise Intervention.
entries.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at high (RCT). Down one for indirectness (healthy adults, muscle-architecture outcome), then down one for imprecision (single small study), giving low.
entries.population: 32 healthy young adults
entries.takeaway: Six weeks of slow-lowering Romanian deadlifts produced hamstring muscle changes similar to Nordic curls, including longer fascicles, so either can build injury-relevant hamstring adaptations.

entries.authors: Visser TSS, Neill SO, Hébert-Losier K, Eygendaal D, de Vos RJ
entries.title: Normative values for calf muscle strength-endurance in the general population assessed with the Calf Raise Application: A large international cross-sectional study.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (cross-sectional normative study). Down one level for indirectness (uninjured adults, not knee rehab), giving very low.
entries.population: 500 adults without Achilles problems or recent leg immobilization, most physically active
entries.takeaway: In 500 generally active adults, the typical single-leg heel raise test reached the mid-20s in reps per leg, with no dominant-side difference; women, less active people and those with higher BMI scored lower.

entries.authors: Hébert-Losier K, Wessman C, Alricsson M, Svantesson U
entries.title: Updated reliability and normative values for the standing heel-rise test in healthy adults.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (cross-sectional normative and reliability study). Down one level for indirectness (uninjured adults), giving very low.
entries.population: 566 community volunteers aged 20-81
entries.takeaway: Single-leg heel raises to fatigue were very repeatable from week to week; typical counts were in the low-to-mid 20s and depended on sex, age, BMI and activity level.

entries.authors: Silva RLE, Pinheiro YT, Lins CAA, de Oliveira RR, Scattone Silva R
entries.title: Assessment of quality of movement during a lateral step-down test: Narrative review.
entries.journal: Journal of bodywork and movement therapies
entries.gradeBasis: Narrative review, so it starts at very low, which is the floor. It is also indirect (mixed populations, no multi-ligament sprain).
entries.population: 16 studies of healthy recruits, athletes, sedentary adults and people with knee or ankle problems
entries.takeaway: The lateral step-down is a simple, moderately reliable way to rate lower-limb movement quality; poorer scores tracked with weaker hip external rotation and knee extension and with stiffer ankles, but test methods vary.

entries.authors: Werner DM, Di Stasi S, Lewis CL, Barrios JA
entries.title: Test-retest reliability and minimum detectable change for various frontal plane projection angles during dynamic tasks.
entries.journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Starts at low (measurement-reliability study). Down one level for indirectness (healthy adults), giving very low. The single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 20 healthy young adults tested twice, 7-14 days apart
entries.takeaway: Knee and hip angles measured from 2D video were moderately to highly repeatable between days; of the tasks tested, the lateral step-down gave the smallest change needed to count as real.

entries.authors: Gomes DA, da Costa GV, Martins EC, Silva DO, Haupenthal A, Ruschel C, de Castro MP, Fontana HB
entries.title: Are visual assessments of the single-leg squat valid to be used in clinical practice? A systematic review of measurement properties based on the COSMIN guideline.
entries.journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine
entries.gradeBasis: The review's own modified GRADE ranges from very low to moderate; we take the lower bound, very low, as for other ranged ratings. Even at the moderate upper bound, the indirectness downgrade (single-leg squat, not lateral step-down) would leave it low.
entries.population: 10 studies of visual single-leg squat rating in mixed populations
entries.takeaway: Eyeball ratings of single-leg squat quality, including medial knee displacement, mostly lacked adequate evidence that they can tell groups apart; only one scale showed discriminative validity, at very low certainty, so visual checks need caution.

entries.authors: Al Attar WSA, Bakhsh JM, Khaledi EH, Ghulam H, Sanders RH
entries.title: Injury prevention programs that include plyometric exercises reduce the incidence of anterior cruciate ligament injury: a systematic review of cluster randomised trials.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts high: systematic review and meta-analysis of cluster RCTs only, and the abstract reports no GRADE rating. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured athletes and an injury-incidence outcome, not rehab after a non-operative multi-ligament sprain. Result: moderate.
entries.population: Uninjured sport participants of any age, sex or level (9 cluster trials, 14,394 people)
entries.takeaway: Across nine cluster trials, warm-up programmes that included jump and landing drills cut ACL injury rates by about 60% compared with usual warm-ups; subgroup estimates suggested the effect holds in males too.

entries.authors: Webster KE, Hewett TE
entries.title: Meta-analysis of meta-analyses of anterior cruciate ligament injury reduction training programs.
entries.journal: Journal of orthopaedic research : official publication of the Orthopaedic Research Society
entries.gradeBasis: No GRADE rating in the abstract. The abstract does not say the pooled studies were randomised, and the prevention meta-analyses it combines also include non-randomised controlled cohorts such as Mandelbaum 2005. So it is not a synthesis of RCTs only, and it starts low. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured, mostly female athletes and an injury-incidence outcome. Result: very low.
entries.population: Uninjured athletes in prevention studies, mostly female (6 of 8 pooled meta-analyses were female-only)
entries.takeaway: Pooling eight earlier meta-analyses, ACL injury prevention training about halved ACL injury risk in athletes overall; most of the data came from female athletes, and the authors judged the male data too thin for a conclusion.

entries.authors: Thorborg K, Krommes KK, Esteve E, Clausen MB, Bartels EM, Rathleff MS
entries.title: Effect of specific exercise-based football injury prevention programmes on the overall injury rate in football: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the FIFA 11 and 11+ programmes.
entries.gradeBasis: Starts high: meta-analysis of cluster RCTs, and the abstract reports no GRADE rating. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured soccer players and an overall-injury outcome, not lacrosse and not rehab. Result: moderate.
entries.population: Uninjured recreational and sub-elite football (soccer) players in 6 cluster RCTs (4 of the FIFA 11+)
entries.takeaway: Pooling four cluster trials in recreational and sub-elite footballers, the FIFA 11+ warm-up cut overall injury rates by about 39%; the two trials of the older FIFA 11 programme showed no clear effect.

entries.authors: Slauterbeck JR, Choquette R, Tourville TW, Krug M, Mandelbaum BR, Vacek P, Beynnon BD.
entries.title: Implementation of the FIFA 11+ Injury Prevention Program by High School Athletic Teams Did Not Reduce Lower Extremity Injuries: A Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Cluster randomized trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured adolescent athletes in several sports and an injury-rate outcome, not rehab. A single trial but a large one, so no imprecision downgrade. Result: moderate.
entries.population: uninjured US high-school athletes in several sports (14 schools, about 3,600 athletes)
entries.takeaway: When high-school coaches delivered the FIFA 11+ across several sports, lower-limb injury rates did not fall compared with usual warm-ups, though only about a third of teams did the full programme twice a week.

entries.authors: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB.
entries.title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials only, so it starts at high (the abstract reports no GRADE rating). Down one level for indirectness: uninjured sport participants and an injury-incidence outcome, not rehab. Result: moderate.
entries.population: uninjured sport participants in 25 randomized trials (26,610 people)
entries.takeaway: Across 25 trials, strength training, balance (proprioception) training and multi-component programmes each reduced sports injuries while stretching did not, and strength training showed the largest effect.

entries.authors: Su W, Wang J, Ying Y, Lu B, Liu H, Zhou Z, Liu C, Yun H.
entries.title: Injury risk reduction programs including balance training reduce the incidence of anterior cruciate ligament injuries in soccer players: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
entries.journal: Journal of orthopaedic surgery and research
entries.gradeBasis: Its eligibility admitted cohort studies as well as trials, and non-randomized studies are among those included, so it starts at low; the full text gives no GRADE rating for the outcome. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured soccer players and an ACL-injury outcome. Result: very low.
entries.population: uninjured male and female soccer players in 8 studies (20,336 people)
entries.takeaway: In eight soccer studies, mostly trials, prevention programmes that included balance exercises were linked to about 58% fewer ACL injuries, with benefit in both the male and female subgroups.

entries.authors: Fitzgerald GK, Axe MJ, Snyder-Mackler L.
entries.title: The efficacy of perturbation training in nonoperative anterior cruciate ligament rehabilitation programs for physical active individuals.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: an isolated ACL or graft rupture with multi-ligament injuries excluded, though like this knee it was managed without surgery. Down one more for a single small study (26 people). Result: low.
entries.population: 26 active people with an ACL or ACL-graft rupture managed without surgery (multi-ligament or meniscal damage needing repair excluded)
entries.takeaway: In active people managing an ACL or graft rupture without surgery, adding support-surface perturbation (balance) training to standard rehab meant fewer rehab failures from giving way, and function held up better at six months.

entries.authors: Arundale AJH, Cummer K, Capin JJ, Zarzycki R, Snyder-Mackler L.
entries.title: Report of the Clinical and Functional Primary Outcomes in Men of the ACL-SPORTS Trial: Similar Outcomes in Men Receiving Secondary Prevention With and Without Perturbation Training 1 and 2 Years After ACL Reconstruction.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: men after ACL reconstruction. Down one more for a single small study (40 men). Result: low.
entries.population: 40 men 3-9 months after ACL reconstruction who already met strength and swelling criteria
entries.takeaway: In men 3-9 months after ACL reconstruction, adding perturbation training to a strengthening, agility and secondary-prevention programme gave no meaningful extra gain in strength, hop symmetry or self-reported knee function.

entries.authors: Arumugam A, Björklund M, Mikko S, Häger CK.
entries.title: Effects of neuromuscular training on knee proprioception in individuals with anterior cruciate ligament injury: a systematic review and GRADE evidence synthesis.
entries.gradeBasis: The review’s own GRADE rates the proprioception evidence very low. That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (post-surgical ACL population) changes nothing.
entries.population: 327 people after ACL reconstruction in 9 small randomized trials
entries.takeaway: Nine small trials after ACL reconstruction showed small, inconsistent effects of neuromuscular or balance training on knee proprioception tests, and with very low certainty no single approach could be recommended.

entries.authors: Negahban H, Mazaheri M, Kingma I, van Dieën JH.
entries.title: A systematic review of postural control during single-leg stance in patients with untreated anterior cruciate ligament injury.
entries.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
entries.gradeBasis: Systematic review of case-control studies, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: isolated ACL injury rather than a multi-ligament sprain, though both were managed without surgery. Result: very low.
entries.population: people with an ACL injury not treated surgically, compared with healthy controls (12 studies)
entries.takeaway: In people with an ACL injury managed without surgery, single-leg stance sway was larger than in healthy controls on both legs, and with eyes closed the injured leg swayed more than the other one.

entries.authors: Yu L, Xue X, Zheng S, Tao W, Li Q, Wang Y, Gu X, Sun Y, Wang R, Hua Y.
entries.title: Failed single-leg assessment of postural stability after anterior cruciate ligament injuries and reconstruction: An updated systematic review and meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of observational comparison studies, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: ACL injury or reconstruction, not a non-operative multi-ligament sprain. Result: very low.
entries.population: people with ACL injury or reconstruction compared with healthy controls (14 studies)
entries.takeaway: An updated pooling of 14 studies found force-plate sway in single-leg stance, eyes open or closed, differed little between ACL-injured or reconstructed knees and healthy controls, apart from a weak eyes-open gap after reconstruction.

entries.authors: Springer BA, Marin R, Cyhan T, Roberts H, Gill NW.
entries.title: Normative values for the unipedal stance test with eyes open and closed.
entries.gradeBasis: Cross-sectional normative study, so it starts at low (Europe PMC tags it as a trial, but it describes a prospective normative sample). Down one level for indirectness: healthy adults, not an injured knee. Result: very low.
entries.population: 549 healthy adults aged 18 to over 80
entries.takeaway: In 549 healthy adults, timed single-leg stance with eyes open and closed, scored as the best of three trials, agreed very closely between raters, fell with age and did not differ by sex.

entries.authors: Chmielewski TL, George SZ, Tillman SM, Moser MW, Lentz TA, Indelicato PA, Trumble TN, Shuster JJ, Cicuttini FM, Leeuwenburgh C.
entries.title: Low- Versus High-Intensity Plyometric Exercise During Rehabilitation After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Down one more for a single small study (24 people). Result: low.
entries.population: 24 adults about 12-18 weeks after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: About 14 weeks after ACL reconstruction, eight weeks of low- or high-intensity running, jumping and agility work gave similar results, and the two groups combined improved in self-reported function, jump height, quadriceps strength and pain.

entries.authors: Buckthorpe M, Della Villa F.
entries.title: Recommendations for Plyometric Training after ACL Reconstruction - A Clinical Commentary.
entries.journal: International journal of sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: Clinical commentary (expert opinion), so it starts at very low, which is the floor. It is also indirect (post-ACL reconstruction).
entries.population: athletes in rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction (a clinical commentary, no participants)
entries.takeaway: This clinical commentary proposes a four-stage plyometric progression matched to recovery, raising intensity gradually through effort, momentum before landing, ground-contact time and surface, with criterion-based monitoring throughout.

entries.authors: Kotsifaki R, Korakakis V, King E, Barbosa O, Maree D, Pantouveris M, Bjerregaard A, Luomajoki J, Wilhelmsen J, Whiteley R.
entries.title: Aspetar clinical practice guideline on rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
entries.gradeBasis: The guideline’s own GRADE rates the plyometric and agility evidence very low, and its return-to-running and return-to-sport criteria rest on clinical experience and consensus (read in the open full text). That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (post-surgical ACL population) changes nothing.
entries.population: patients in rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction (a guideline built on trials and systematic reviews)
entries.takeaway: This GRADE-based guideline after ACL reconstruction found plyometric and agility training may improve function (very low certainty), judged it unclear whether passing a test battery lowers reinjury, and based its return criteria on experience and consensus.

entries.authors: Alexander JLN, Culvenor AG, Johnston RRT, Ezzat AM, Barton CJ.
entries.title: Strategies to prevent and manage running-related knee injuries: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials.
entries.gradeBasis: The review rates graduated running programmes very low to low certainty (GRADE); we take the lower bound, very low. That is already the floor, so the indirectness downgrade (uninjured runners and running-related knee injury, not a ligament sprain) changes nothing.
entries.population: novice and recreational runners in 30 randomized trials of preventing or managing running-related knee injury
entries.takeaway: In trials of novice and recreational runners, graduated running programmes did not clearly change knee injury risk (very low to low certainty), though one low-certainty trial suggested that retraining to land more softly cut knee injuries.

entries.authors: Kerr ZY, Quigley A, Yeargin SW, Lincoln AE, Mensch J, Caswell SV, Dompier TP.
entries.title: The epidemiology of NCAA men's lacrosse injuries, 2009/10-2014/15 academic years.
entries.gradeBasis: Descriptive injury-surveillance cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured players and an injury-rate outcome, not rehab or return after a sprain. Result: very low.
entries.population: US college men’s lacrosse players (25 programmes, 63 team-seasons)
entries.takeaway: In NCAA men’s lacrosse from 2009 to 2015, most injuries were to the lower limb, sprains and strains were the commonest diagnoses, and games carried about three times the practice injury rate.

entries.authors: Ardern CL, Taylor NF, Feller JA, Webster KE.
entries.title: A systematic review of the psychological factors associated with returning to sport following injury.
entries.gradeBasis: Systematic review of observational studies with no GRADE reported, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: mixed sports injuries, not a non-operative knee sprain. Result: very low.
entries.population: athletes returning after a range of sports injuries (11 studies, 983 athletes)
entries.takeaway: Across 11 studies of injured athletes, motivation, confidence and low fear of reinjury went with returning to pre-injury sport more often and sooner, though fear was still common at the point of return.

entries.authors: Xiao M, van Niekerk M, Trivedi NN, Hwang CE, Sherman SL, Safran MR, Abrams GD.
entries.title: Patients Who Return to Sport After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Have Significantly Higher Psychological Readiness: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of 3744 Patients.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of non-randomized comparison studies (levels 1-3), so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 3,744 patients after primary ACL reconstruction (16 studies)
entries.takeaway: Across 16 studies after ACL reconstruction, people who returned to sport scored about 21 points higher on the ACL-RSI and lower on kinesiophobia, though their knee-function scores were clinically similar.

entries.authors: Liu Y, Sun Y, Cao M, Wang D, Wang L, Fong DTP, Yung PS, Qiu J.
entries.title: Hop Test Performance is Associated with Return-to-Sport but Shows Limited Association with Reinjury after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: The review itself rates the evidence on 90% hop symmetry and return to sport low certainty (modified GRADE). Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population, not a non-operative multi-ligament sprain. Result: very low.
entries.population: adults after primary one-sided ACL reconstruction (43 studies, about 17,000 people)
entries.takeaway: Pooling 43 studies after ACL reconstruction, reaching 90% symmetry on the single and crossover hops went with modestly higher odds of returning to sport, but hop distance alone may not predict reinjury; certainty was low.

entries.authors: Girdwood MA, Crossley KM, Rio EK, Patterson BE, Haberfield MJ, Couch JL, Mentiplay BF, Hedger M, Culvenor AG.
entries.title: Hop to It! A Systematic Review and Longitudinal Meta-analysis of Hop Performance After ACL Reconstruction.
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of mostly observational studies with no formal GRADE (its methods say why), so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: people after primary ACL reconstruction, aged 18-40 on average, in studies of at least 50 (136 studies, about 23,000 people)
entries.takeaway: Across 136 studies after ACL reconstruction, hop symmetry rose steeply early then levelled off after 18-24 months; forward hop tests tracked one another closely, while vertical and side hops showed the largest deficits.

entries.authors: Webster KE, Hewett TE.
entries.title: What is the Evidence for and Validity of Return-to-Sport Testing after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of observational cohorts with no GRADE reported, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: people after ACL reconstruction who took return-to-sport test batteries (18 studies)
entries.takeaway: Only about a quarter of patients passed return-to-sport test batteries after ACL reconstruction; passing went with fewer graft ruptures but not fewer ACL injuries overall, and with more opposite-knee injuries, so battery validity is equivocal.

entries.authors: Losciale JM, Bullock G, Cromwell C, Ledbetter L, Pietrosimone L, Sell TC.
entries.title: Hop Testing Lacks Strong Association With Key Outcome Variables After Primary Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Systematic review of observational studies with no GRADE reported, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: people after primary ACL reconstruction (21 studies, about 4,500 patients)
entries.takeaway: Across 21 studies after ACL reconstruction, hop tests related only fairly to self-reported knee function (KOOS, IKDC) and to returning to sport; evidence was insufficient to link them to reinjury, so their predictive value is unestablished.

entries.authors: Grindem H, Engebretsen L, Axe M, Snyder-Mackler L, Risberg MA.
entries.title: Activity and functional readiness, not age, are the critical factors for second anterior cruciate ligament injury - the Delaware-Oslo ACL cohort study.
entries.gradeBasis: Prospective cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 213 athletes followed two years after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In 213 athletes followed two years after ACL reconstruction, passing a 90% return-to-sport battery (questionnaires, quadriceps strength, hop symmetry) was independently linked to far fewer second ACL injuries, while age was not.

entries.authors: Noyes FR, Barber SD, Mangine RE.
entries.title: Abnormal lower limb symmetry determined by function hop tests after anterior cruciate ligament rupture.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Diagnostic-accuracy study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: ACL rupture, not a multi-ligament sprain. A single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 67 patients with ruptured, unreconstructed ACLs
entries.takeaway: In 67 patients with ruptured, unreconstructed ACLs, one-legged hop tests missed many functional deficits (low sensitivity) but rarely flagged a normal limb (high specificity); combining two hop tests caught more abnormal limbs.

entries.authors: Reid A, Birmingham TB, Stratford PW, Alcock GK, Giffin JR.
entries.title: Hop testing provides a reliable and valid outcome measure during rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
entries.gradeBasis: Observational measurement study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. A single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 42 people aged 15-45 about 16 weeks after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In 42 people aged 15-45 four months after ACL reconstruction, the single, triple, crossover and 6-metre timed hops gave reliable symmetry scores that tracked recovery; a change smaller than roughly 7-13 percentage points may just be measurement noise.

entries.authors: Wood A, Hargreaves M, Manfredi JN, Harrell M, Marks Benson E, Rahaman C, Dayal D, Brabston EW, Evely T, Casp A, Momaya AM.
entries.title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Return to Sport Testing Passing Rates for Healthy People: A Systematic Review.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Systematic review of observational studies with no GRADE reported, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured people and a pass-rate outcome. Result: very low.
entries.population: healthy people with no history of ACL injury (32 studies, about 1,550 controls)
entries.takeaway: Across 32 studies of people with no ACL injury, a sizeable share failed common return-to-sport hop, strength and balance tests, and some had natural side-to-side differences above 10%, so a missed 90% line is not automatically pathology.

entries.authors: Fitzgerald GK, Axe MJ, Snyder-Mackler L.
entries.title: A decision-making scheme for returning patients to high-level activity with nonoperative treatment after anterior cruciate ligament rupture.
entries.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
entries.gradeBasis: Cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: isolated ACL rupture, not a multi-ligament sprain, though managed without surgery. A single small study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 93 consecutive patients with an acute one-sided ACL rupture considered for non-operative care
entries.takeaway: A screening exam of four one-legged hop tests, giving-way episodes and two self-reports sorted acute ACL ruptures into rehabilitation candidates; most candidates who tried returned to pre-injury activity without further instability.

entries.authors: Webster KE, Feller JA, Lambros C.
entries.title: Development and preliminary validation of a scale to measure the psychological impact of returning to sport following anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction surgery.
entries.journal: Physical therapy in sport : official journal of the Association of Chartered Physiotherapists in Sports Medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Cross-sectional validation study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 220 people 8-22 months after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: The 12-item ACL-RSI, which asks about emotions, confidence in performance and appraisal of risk, showed high internal consistency in 220 people after ACL reconstruction and scored lower in those who had given up sport.

entries.authors: Webster KE, Feller JA.
entries.title: Development and Validation of a Short Version of the Anterior Cruciate Ligament Return to Sport After Injury (ACL-RSI) Scale.
entries.gradeBasis: Validation study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: two cohorts after ACL reconstruction (535 and 250 patients)
entries.takeaway: In large ACL-reconstruction cohorts, a 6-item short ACL-RSI performed about as well as the full 12-item scale; six-month scores from either version predicted twelve-month return to sport with fair-to-good accuracy.

entries.authors: McPherson AL, Feller JA, Hewett TE, Webster KE.
entries.title: Psychological Readiness to Return to Sport Is Associated With Second Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population, with the cut-off derived only in patients aged 20 or under. A cut-off from one subgroup of one study would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: 329 patients who returned to sport after ACL reconstruction; the cut-off comes from those aged 20 or under
entries.takeaway: The often-quoted ACL-RSI cut-off near 76 comes from this cohort: in patients aged 20 or under, a year after reconstruction, short-version scores below it flagged most later second ACL injuries; scores did not separate older patients.

entries.authors: Piussi R, Simonson R, Högberg J, Thomeé R, Samuelsson K, Hamrin Senorski E.
entries.title: Psychological Patient-reported Outcomes Cannot Predict a Second Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury in Patients who Return to Sports after an Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction.
entries.journal: International journal of sports physical therapy
entries.gradeBasis: Prognostic registry study, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 641 patients, mean age about 25, who returned to sport after ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In 641 patients after ACL reconstruction, no cut-off on the ACL-RSI, KOOS Sport/Rec or QOL, or knee self-efficacy scale separated those who had a second ACL injury within two years of returning.

entries.authors: Sadeqi M, Klouche S, Bohu Y, Herman S, Lefevre N, Gerometta A.
entries.title: Progression of the Psychological ACL-RSI Score and Return to Sport After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Prospective 2-Year Follow-up Study From the French Prospective Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Cohort Study (FAST).
entries.gradeBasis: Prospective cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 681 athletes over 16 followed two years after primary or revision ACL reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In 681 athletes followed two years after ACL reconstruction, ACL-RSI scores rose steadily and were strongly tied to returning to the same sport; the best thresholds found here sat in the 60s, not 76.

entries.authors: Sell TC, Zerega R, King V, Reiter CR, Wrona H, Bullock GS, Mills N, Räisänen A, Ledbetter L, Collins GS, Kvist J, Filbay SR, Losciale JM.
entries.title: Anterior Cruciate Ligament Return to Sport after Injury Scale (ACL-RSI) Scores over Time After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of mostly observational studies; the authors rate certainty weak or limited (not GRADE words), so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: people after ACL tear and reconstruction (83 studies)
entries.takeaway: Pooling 83 mostly high-risk-of-bias studies, ACL-RSI scores rose early after ACL injury and surgery, then changed little until two or more years out; certainty of this evidence was weak or limited throughout.

entries.authors: Webster KE, McPherson AL, Hewett TE, Feller JA.
entries.title: Factors Associated With a Return to Preinjury Level of Sport Performance After Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Surgery.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL population. Result: very low.
entries.population: 222 patients assessed 12 months after ACL reconstruction and followed for 2-4 years
entries.takeaway: Among 222 patients assessed a year after ACL reconstruction, higher ACL-RSI psychological readiness was the only factor that independently predicted returning to pre-injury sport performance; hop symmetry did not survive adjustment.

entries.authors: Hamrin Senorski R, Piussi R, Högberg J, Thomeé R, Samuelsson K, Hamrin Senorski E.
entries.title: Rehabilitation alone after anterior cruciate ligament injury yields greater limb symmetry but lower knee related self-efficacy without limiting return to preinjury activity level.
entries.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
entries.gradeBasis: Registry cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: isolated ACL injury, not a multi-ligament sprain. The non-operative group is small, which would also qualify for imprecision, but very low is the floor.
entries.population: people 15 or older after a first ACL injury: 31 treated with rehabilitation alone, 359 with reconstruction
entries.takeaway: In a Swedish registry, 31 people treated with rehabilitation alone after ACL injury regained more symmetrical thigh strength than reconstructed patients yet reported lower future knee self-efficacy, so symmetry and trust can diverge.

entries.authors: Cuyul-Vásquez I, Álvarez E, Riquelme A, Zimmermann R, Araya-Quintanilla F.
entries.title: Effectiveness of Unilateral Training of the Uninjured Limb on Muscle Strength and Knee Function of Patients With Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Cross-Education.
entries.gradeBasis: The review’s own GRADE rates isometric quadriceps strength at 8-12 weeks high certainty. Down one level for indirectness: post-surgical ACL patients, not a non-operative multi-ligament sprain. Result: moderate.
entries.population: adults after ACL reconstruction in 7 randomized trials
entries.takeaway: Adding training of the uninjured leg to standard rehab after ACL surgery improved quadriceps strength in the operated leg at 8 to 12 weeks; effects on self-reported knee function were inconsistent.

entries.authors: Valdés O, Chalchat E, Rehbein C, Núñez O, García-Vicencio S, Martin V, Ramirez-Campillo R, Peñailillo L.
entries.title: Cross-Education Effect on Force Production Capacity After Unilateral Resistance Training in Clinical Populations: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis.
entries.gradeBasis: The review’s own GRADE rates maximal strength overall moderate certainty. Down one level for indirectness: mixed clinical and immobilisation models, not a knee sprain. Result: low.
entries.population: healthy people with an immobilised limb, people with musculoskeletal conditions and people after stroke (24 controlled trials)
entries.takeaway: Training one limb raised strength in the untrained limb overall, clearest in immobilisation and stroke models; in musculoskeletal patients and lower-limb protocols the effect was not statistically significant.

entries.authors: Spiering BA, Mujika I, Sharp MA, Foulis SA.
entries.title: Maintaining Physical Performance: The Minimal Dose of Exercise Needed to Preserve Endurance and Strength Over Time.
entries.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
entries.gradeBasis: Brief narrative review, so it starts at very low, which is the floor. It is also indirect: a healthy general population, not injured athletes.
entries.population: healthy general populations (too few data on athletes to be specific)
entries.takeaway: Strength and endurance can be held for weeks to months on much less training, as little as one strength session a week, provided intensity stays up; intensity is the key variable to keep.

entries.authors: American College of Sports Medicine.
entries.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults.
entries.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
entries.gradeBasis: A position stand without its own GRADE rating, so it is read as expert consensus and starts at very low, which is the floor. It is also indirect: healthy adults, not training around a knee injury.
entries.population: healthy adults, novice to advanced
entries.takeaway: This position stand recommends multi-joint exercises, 8 to 12 rep loads for novices, and adding about 2 to 10 percent load once the current load can be lifted for one or two reps beyond the target.

entries.authors: Zazulak BT, Hewett TE, Reeves NP, Goldberg B, Cholewicki J.
entries.title: Deficits in neuromuscular control of the trunk predict knee injury risk: a prospective biomechanical-epidemiologic study.
entries.journal: The American journal of sports medicine
entries.gradeBasis: Prospective cohort, so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: uninjured athletes, and it predicts a first injury rather than recovery. Result: very low.
entries.population: 277 uninjured college athletes followed for 3 years
entries.takeaway: Athletes whose trunks moved more after a sudden release, especially sideways, were more likely to injure knee ligaments later; the prediction held in women, while in men only past low back pain predicted it.

entries.authors: Ellestad SH, Holcomb TP, Swiergol AM, Holmstrup ME, Dicus JR.
entries.title: The Quantification of Muscle Activation During the Loaded Carry Movement Pattern.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized-order within-subject trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: healthy young adults and a muscle-activation outcome. Down one more for a single small study (18 usable of 26). Result: low.
entries.population: 18 healthy college-age adults with usable data (26 recruited)
entries.takeaway: Walking with dumbbells activated the abdominal and low-back muscles more than holding the same weights still, and a one-sided carry added extra activity on the loaded side.

entries.authors: McCrary JM, Ackermann BJ, Halaki M.
entries.title: A systematic review of the effects of upper body warm-up on performance and injury.
entries.gradeBasis: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials only, so it starts at high (no GRADE reported). Down one level for indirectness: healthy people, upper-body warm-ups and performance outcomes. Result: moderate.
entries.population: healthy people in 31 randomized trials of upper-body warm-ups
entries.takeaway: High-load dynamic warm-ups improved strength and power performance, brief static stretching did nothing for power, and no trial looked at whether upper-body warm-ups prevent injury.

entries.authors: Ribeiro AS, Romanzini M, Schoenfeld BJ, Souza MF, Avelar A, Cyrino ES.
entries.title: Effect of different warm-up procedures on the performance of resistance training exercises.
entries.gradeBasis: Randomized crossover trial, so it starts at high. Down one level for indirectness: healthy men and a reps-to-failure outcome. Down one more for a single small study (15 men). Result: low.
entries.population: 15 men doing bench press, squat and arm curl to failure
entries.takeaway: Specific, aerobic or combined warm-ups did not change total reps or fatigue across four sets at 80% of max compared with no warm-up.

entries.authors: Wilson CJ, Nunes JP, Blazevich AJ.
entries.title: The effect of muscle warm-up on voluntary and evoked force-time parameters: A systematic review and meta-analysis with meta-regression.
entries.journal: Journal of sport and health science
entries.gradeBasis: Meta-analysis of experiments that were not all randomized (no GRADE reported), so it starts at low. Down one level for indirectness: healthy adults, and muscle temperature and force outcomes. Result: very low.
entries.population: healthy adults aged 18 to 60 in 33 experimental studies (921 participants)
entries.takeaway: Warming muscle improved fast force and power but not maximum force, and active warm-ups did no better than passive heating.

gateRationales.why: Loading through pain that stays within set limits and settles by the next morning is the pain-monitoring model tested in tendon injuries; two clean weeks is the app’s adaptation, not a published threshold.

After ACL surgery a single-leg strength comparison catches deficits that hop tests can hide, and return-to-running protocols that used symmetry usually set it above 70%; ratios can still flatter recovery when the good leg has weakened too.

After ACL surgery running usually restarts on time alone, though clinicians commonly also want low pain and minimal swelling, and more activity went with more swelling; the 4-mile, no-reaction test itself has no published source.

The lateral step-down is a moderately reliable movement-quality check and 2D video angles repeat between days, but eyeball ratings are coarse, and in healthy people hip weakness was mostly not linked to knee collapse, so it checks knee control directly.

After ACL surgery more symmetrical quadriceps strength before return went with fewer reinjuries, a single-leg leg press max was highly repeatable in athletes, and ratios can flatter recovery when the good leg has weakened too.
After ACL surgery the Bulgarian split squat let the back leg take load from the operated one, so equal loads side to side don’t prove the injured knee did equal work.
Single-leg heel raises to fatigue are a very repeatable count, and healthy adults typically reach the low-to-mid 20s per leg with no side difference, so 20 each side sits a little below typical.

A clinician’s knee-swelling grade is reliable and offered as a progression signal, swelling induced in healthy volunteers lowered quadriceps strength, and lingering swelling after ACL surgery went with weaker quadriceps later; a self-checked version is untested.

Athletes who returned with more symmetrical thigh strength had fewer reinjuries after ACL surgery, but passing such criteria is not clearly protective and deficits on average outlast a year, so the line is a minimum.

More activity went with more swelling after ACL surgery, and swelling induced in healthy volunteers lowered quadriceps strength, so the morning after the hardest loading is the check; a self-checked version is untested.

Experts advise deciding return to sport together with clinicians, a multi-ligament consensus notes the literature generally favours surgery, and passing tests is not clearly protective, so a specialist signs off before contact.

After an ACL injury managed without surgery the injured leg swayed more with eyes closed, a newer pooling found only small differences, and healthy adults’ best-of-three times agreed very closely between raters; the 30 s line is the program’s own.

In unreconstructed ACL ruptures the hop battery missed some deficits but rarely flagged a normal leg, and after ACL surgery 90% symmetry went with returning to sport while its link to reinjury stayed weak.
After ACL surgery the forward hops tracked one another closely and gave repeatable symmetry scores, though a change under roughly 7-13 points may be noise and some uninjured people miss a 90% line.

After ACL surgery passing a 90% battery that included hops went with fewer second ACL injuries in one cohort, but across studies battery validity was equivocal, and readiness predicted return to performance where hop symmetry did not.

The 6-meter timed hop gave repeatable symmetry scores after ACL surgery, and a screen combining four hops with giving-way and self-reports helped sort unreconstructed ACL ruptures, but no study found tests the timed hop’s own 90% line.

The 76 line comes from one post-surgery cohort that used the 6-item short form, in patients 20 or under, to flag second injuries; the app scores the full 12-item form, and other cohorts’ return-to-sport lines sat in the 60s.

Across injured athletes confidence and low fear went with returning to sport, after ACL surgery psychological readiness predicted return to performance, and ACL tears treated by rehab alone regained symmetry while self-efficacy lagged, so trust is asked separately.
